bubble_sort.description: Bubble sort is a way to put numbers in order. You compare two numbers at a time and swap them if they're not in the right order. Keep doing this until all the numbers are in the correct order. It's like making the biggest numbers "bubble" to the end.
bubble_sort.instructions: Click on the bubbles in the green area to pop them. Put them in the right order (from smallest to biggest) and Beat the Algorithm! The Reset button deletes your current attempt. Choose a difficulty and press start. Good Luck!

detailedDescription.simpleExplanation: Bubble sort is a simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through a list of elements, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. The algorithm gets its name from the way smaller elements "bubble" to the top of the list. This process is repeated until the entire list is sorted.

steps.step2: Compare neighboring values from left to right.
steps.step3: Swap them if the left value is larger; otherwise leave them in place.
steps.step4: After one pass, the largest remaining value is in its final position.
steps.step5: Repeat on the remaining unsorted part, shortening each pass.
steps.step6: If a pass makes no swaps, the whole list is already sorted.
steps.step7: Finish with all values in ascending order.

detailedDescription.timeComplexity: Bubble sort takes O(n?) time on average and in the worst case. With the early-exit check used here, an already sorted list needs one pass and takes O(n) time.
detailedDescription.spaceComplexity: Bubble sort has a space complexity of O(1), as it performs sorting in-place without requiring additional memory beyond the input array.
detailedDescription.realWorldApplications: Bubble sort is rarely used in production code due to its poor performance, but it finds applications in educational contexts for teaching sorting concepts, and in scenarios with very small datasets or nearly sorted data where its simplicity is beneficial.

selection_sort.description: Selection sort is a way to put numbers in order. You find the smallest number and put it in the first position. Then, you find the next smallest number and put it in the second position. Repeat this until all the numbers are sorted.
selection_sort.instructions: Select a number by clicking it. This will select the value and you can put it in the correct box. Put them in the right order (from smallest to biggest) and Beat the Algorithm! Choose a difficulty and press start. Good Luck!

detailedDescription.simpleExplanation: Selection sort is a simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly finds the minimum element from the unsorted part of the list and places it at the beginning. The algorithm divides the list into two parts: the sorted part at the left end and the unsorted part at the right end. Initially, the sorted part is empty, and the entire list is unsorted.

steps.step1: Start with the entire list unsorted.
steps.step2: Treat the first unsorted value as the current minimum.
steps.step3: Compare it with every later value and update the minimum when a smaller one is found.
steps.step4: Swap the minimum with the first unsorted value, if they are different positions.
steps.step5: Grow the sorted prefix by one and repeat until the list is sorted.

detailedDescription.timeComplexity: Selection sort has a time complexity of O(n^2) in the average and worst cases, where n is the number of elements in the list. Similar to bubble sort, it is not considered an efficient sorting algorithm for large lists. But, it is considered more efficient than bubble sort because of the number of swaps done by each.
detailedDescription.spaceComplexity: Selection sort has a space complexity of O(1), as it performs sorting in-place without requiring additional memory beyond the input array.
detailedDescription.realWorldApplications: Selection sort is useful when the cost of swapping elements is high, as it performs at most n-1 swaps. It is commonly used in scenarios with small datasets, embedded systems with limited memory, and when stability is not a requirement.

heap_sort.description: Heap sort builds a max heap, a binary tree in which each parent is at least as large as its children. It repeatedly moves the largest value at the root to the end of the active heap, shrinks the heap, and restores its structure. The resulting list is sorted from smallest to largest.
heap_sort.instructions: Select a number by clicking it. This will select the value and you can put it in the correct box. If there is a value in that box, that value will be put into the selection box. Put them in the right order (from smallest to biggest) and Beat the Algorithm! Choose a difficulty and press start. Good Luck!

detailedDescription.simpleExplanation: Heap sort builds a max heap, a binary tree in which each parent is at least as large as its children. It repeatedly moves the largest value at the root to the end of the active heap, shrinks the heap, and restores its structure. The resulting list is sorted from smallest to largest.

steps.step1: Start with the values in array order, viewed as a complete binary tree.
steps.step2: Build a max heap: each parent is at least as large as its children.
steps.step3: Start at the last non-leaf node and sift down each subtree toward the root.
steps.step4: The root now holds the largest value in the active heap.
steps.step5: Swap the root with the last value in the active heap, putting the maximum in its final position.
steps.step6: Shrink the heap by one; the sorted suffix stays outside the heap.
steps.step7: Sift the new root down, swapping with its larger child until the max-heap property is restored.
steps.step8: Repeat extraction and repair until the whole array is sorted in ascending order.

detailedDescription.timeComplexity: Building a max heap takes O(n) time. Repeatedly extracting the maximum and restoring the heap takes O(n log n) time overall in the average and worst cases. Each sift-down operation takes at most O(log n).
detailedDescription.spaceComplexity: Heap sort has a space complexity of O(1), as it performs sorting in-place using the input array itself to build the heap structure.
detailedDescription.realWorldApplications: Heap sort is useful when predictable O(n log n) worst-case time and constant auxiliary space matter. The underlying heap data structure also powers priority queues and top-k selection; those applications do not require sorting the entire list.

merge_sort.description: Merge sort works by dividing the list into smaller parts, sorting them individually, and then merging them back together to obtain a sorted list. It uses the idea of dividing and merging to efficiently sort the numbers.
merge_sort.instructions: Select a number by clicking it. This will select the value and put it in the white list of values on top. You can remove the values from the list on top by clicking it. Put them in the right order (from smallest to biggest) and Beat the Algorithm! Choose a difficulty and press start. Good Luck!

detailedDescription.simpleExplanation: This visualization uses bottom-up merge sort. It starts with sorted runs of one value, merges neighboring runs, and doubles their size after each pass until a single sorted run covers the list. Equal values are taken from the left run first, making the algorithm stable.

steps.step1: Start with an unsorted list; each individual value is a sorted run of length one.
steps.step2: Take adjacent sorted runs in pairs.
steps.step3: Compare the front values of the two runs and take the smaller value next.
steps.step4: On equal values, take from the left run first to preserve stability.
steps.step5: Append any leftover values and write the merged run back into the list.
steps.step6: After a pass, double the run size and repeat; an unpaired last run carries forward.
steps.step7: Stop when one sorted run covers the entire list.

detailedDescription.timeComplexity: Merge sort has a time complexity of O(n log n) in all cases, where n is the number of elements in the list. It is an efficient sorting algorithm and guarantees consistent performance, making it suitable for large lists. However, merge sort requires additional space to store temporary sublists during the merging process.
detailedDescription.spaceComplexity: Merge sort has a space complexity of O(n), as it requires additional memory equal to the size of the input array to store temporary sublists during the merging process.
detailedDescription.realWorldApplications: Merge sort is widely used in external sorting for large datasets that don't fit in memory, stable sorting requirements, and parallel processing environments. It is commonly used in programming languages' standard libraries, database systems, and file sorting applications.

quick_sort.description: Quick sort chooses a pivot and partitions the list around it: values at or below the pivot go to the left, and larger values go to the right. Once the pivot is in its final position, it repeats the process on each side.
quick_sort.instructions: Select two numbers to swap their places. Arrange your row from smallest to largest before the computer finishes. Select the same number again to cancel your selection, or press Reset to restore your original row. Your moves do not have to follow the computer's partitioning strategy.

detailedDescription.simpleExplanation: This visualization uses quick sort with Lomuto partitioning. The last value in the active partition is the pivot. Scan the other values and move each value at or below the pivot into the left part. Then place the pivot between that part and the larger values. The pivot is now in its final position; recursively sort the parts on either side. Partitions with one value are already finished. This swapping version is not stable: equal values may change their relative order.

steps.step1: Start with the entire list as the active partition.
steps.step2: Choose the last value of the active partition as the pivot.
steps.step3: Scan from left to right, comparing each remaining value with the pivot.
steps.step4: When a value is at or below the pivot, swap it into the next slot in the left part if needed. Leave larger values for the right part.
steps.step5: Place the pivot immediately after the left part. It is now in its final position and will not move again.
steps.step6: Repeat the process on the left partition, then the right partition, excluding the fixed pivot.
steps.step7: Stop at empty or single-value partitions. When every partition is finished, the list is sorted.

detailedDescription.timeComplexity: Quick sort takes O(n log n) time on average when partitions are reasonably balanced. Its worst case is O(n^2). With the last-value pivot used here, already sorted, reverse-sorted, and all-equal lists create unbalanced partitions and reach that worst case. Randomized pivots and other partitioning strategies can help in practical implementations.
detailedDescription.spaceComplexity: Partitioning is in place and uses O(1) auxiliary space. Recursive calls use O(log n) stack space on average and O(n) in the worst case. The saved animation frames use additional memory for visualization and are separate from the algorithm's auxiliary space.
detailedDescription.realWorldApplications: Quick sort is useful for sorting arrays in memory when good average performance matters and equal values do not need to retain their original order. Its partitioning idea also underlies quickselect, which finds an order statistic such as the median without sorting the entire array. Practical sorting implementations often combine partitioning with other methods to handle small partitions and avoid poor worst-case behavior.
